How many nights can a power station run my CPAP?

Scenarios Updated 2026-08-01

Between roughly one night and five on the same battery, and the variable is the humidifier rather than the machine. The manufacturer’s own power-consumption table gives three figures for one popular unit: blower only, blower with humidifier, and blower with humidifier and heated tube — and the third is several times the first.

So the question "how many nights" cannot be answered by battery size alone. Turn humidification off and a small machine covers multiple nights; leave it and the heated tube on and the same battery covers one.

Open the runtime calculator →

This page states electrical facts only — measured draw, waveform requirements and computed runtimes. It is not medical advice and makes no claim about whether any setup is suitable for therapy. For questions about your device, your therapy or travelling with either, ask the device manufacturer and your clinician.

The one waveform requirement we can cite

ResMed states in its own battery-power guide that its devices require a pure sine wave inverter, and recommends an inverter rated for far more continuous power than the machine actually draws. The same document carries a warning that its heated humidifiers, outside a short listed exception, must not be used with inverters at all. That is a manufacturer instruction with a document behind it, and it is the reason a waveform check appears in our verdict for this load. Another manufacturer’s battery-powered devices disable humidification automatically and say so in the manual. Read your own device’s documentation: these instructions differ by brand and by model, and none of them can be inferred from the electrical figures.

What the device maker asks for

The manufacturer’s inverter recommendation, alongside what the machine measurably draws. The gap between them is deliberate headroom on their part, not a contradiction.

Planning for more than one night

Two things make a multi-night plan behave worse than the arithmetic suggests, and both are avoidable. The first is leaving the station switched on all day between sessions: its own idle consumption is a continuous load, and over three days of daylight it can cost more than a night of therapy. Switch the machine off in the morning if it is not doing anything else. The second is the inverter itself. Running a small load through a mains inverter is the least efficient thing a power station does — the conversion loss is roughly fixed while the load is tiny, so a low-wattage device pays a disproportionate share of it. Feeding the device from a direct-current output instead removes that loss entirely, and it is also the route the device makers recommend first.

If the trip is longer than the battery, the answer is a recharge plan rather than a bigger battery. A modest panel replaces a night of the humidifier-on figure in a few good hours, which is a far lighter thing to carry than the equivalent extra capacity. The solar calculator will tell you whether your panel and your machine can actually do that together, because the answer depends on the voltage window as much as on the wattage.

The DC route, which avoids the question

Most CPAP makers sell a DC converter that feeds the machine directly from a 12 V or 24 V source, skipping the inverter entirely. That removes the waveform question, removes the inverter’s conversion loss, and is what the manufacturers themselves recommend first. If you are buying a power station for this, a DC output that matches your device’s converter is worth more than a larger battery.

Questions people ask

What size power station do I need for a CPAP machine?
Work from your own configuration. With humidification off, one night is a small fraction of a compact power station; with humidifier and heated tube it is several times that. Multiply your configuration’s nightly figure by the nights you need, add the station’s own idle consumption for the same period, and compare against usable capacity rather than the nameplate.
Does turning the humidifier off really make that much difference?
On the manufacturer’s measured table for one common device family, the blower alone is a small fraction of the same machine with humidifier and heated tube running. Heating water and heating a tube are both resistive loads; the blower is not. It is the single largest lever you have.
Do I need a pure sine wave inverter?
One manufacturer states so explicitly in its battery guide, along with a warning against running its heated humidifiers from inverters at all. That is the documentation we can cite. Check what your own device maker publishes rather than generalising from it.
